Esther — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The book of Esther shows God's care for the Jews who had been scattered among the peoples of a foreign empire.

He preserved them wonderfully when they faced destruction.

Although God's name does not appear in the book, his providential hand can be seen in the smallest events that contributed to the deliverance of his people.

The events belong historically between Ezra chapters 6 and 7.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe royal feast of Ahasuerus.1–9Vashti's refusal to appear, The king's decree.10–22
Ahasuerus holds a royal feast (verses 1–9)

Pride rose in Ahasuerus's heart as his kingdom became magnificent, and he gave an extravagant feast.

This was an exhibition of empty self-glory.

A simple meal of vegetables enjoyed in peace is better than an enormous banquet of wine accompanied by noise and disorder.

Unless grace rules a person's heart, self-exaltation and self-indulgence will govern life in one form or another.

Yet the king did not require anyone to drink. Those who became drunk had only themselves to blame.

Even this precaution by a pagan ruler should shame many who call themselves Christians.

Some pressure their companions into drinking to excess under the pretense of celebrating one another's health.

In doing so they encourage sin and bring spiritual death alongside it.

God's warning against such people is serious (Habakkuk 2:15–16).

Let them read it and tremble.

Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 2 Corinthians 2:16.Verified editorial cross-reference: Hab.2.16.
Vashti refuses; the king makes a decree (verses 10–22)

Through his own folly Ahasuerus turned his festival into distress.

Special celebrations often end with trouble and annoyance.

People in authority should be careful not to give commands that others may reasonably refuse to obey.

When wine governs a person, sound judgment is lost.

Ahasuerus ruled 127 provinces but could not govern his own temper.

Whether the decree served his anger or his political interests, divine Providence used it to prepare the way for Esther to become queen.

God was already defeating Haman's wicked plot before Haman even imagined it or rose to power.

We should rejoice that the Lord reigns.

He can overrule human frenzy and foolishness to accomplish his own glory and secure his people's welfare and happiness.

[Esth.1.1-Esth.1.9]
Esther
We find in this book, that even those Jews who were scattered in the province of the heathen, were taken care of, and were wonderfully preserved, when threatened with destruction. Though the name of God be not in this book, the finger of God is shown by minute events for the bringing about his people's deliverance. This history comes in between Ezr 6; 7.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The royal feast of Ahasuerus. | (1-9) |
Vashti's refusal to appear, The king's decree. | (10-22) |
Verses 1-9
The pride of Ahasuerus's heart rising with the grandeur of his kingdom, he made an extravagant feast. This was vain glory. Better is a dinner of herbs with quietness, than this banquet of wine, with all the noise and tumult that must have attended it. But except grace prevails in the heart, self-exaltation and self-indulgence, in one form or another, will be the ruling principle. Yet none did compel; so that if any drank to excess, it was their own fault. This caution of a heathen prince, even when he would show his generosity, may shame many called Christians, who, under pretence of sending the health round, send sin round, and death with it. There is a woe to them that do so; let them read it, and tremble, [Hab.2.15] Ha 2:15, [2Cor.2.16] 16.
[Esth.1.10-Esth.1.22]
Verses 10-22
Ahasuerus's feast ended in heaviness, by his own folly. Seasons of peculiar festivity often end in vexation. Superiors should be careful not to command what may reasonably be disobeyed. But when wine is in, men's reason departs from them. He that had rule over 127 provinces, had no rule over his own spirit. But whether the passion or the policy of the king was served by this decree, God's providence made way for Esther to the crown, and defeated Haman's wicked project, even before it had entered into his heart, and he arrived at his power. Let us rejoice that the Lord reigns, and will overrule the madness or folly of mankind to promote his own glory, and the safety and happiness of his people.

Esther becomes queen (verses 1–20)

Without divine revelation, people have often embraced unreasonable social practices.

The arrangement described here shows the need for the gospel of Jesus Christ, which cleanses people of sinful desires and calls them back to the original design of marriage.

Esther was chosen as queen.

Henry warns against accusing her of sin merely for entering this situation without understanding the customs of the time and region.

In Henry's account of those customs, any woman whom the king took became his wife, though she might hold a lower rank than the queen.

How far human nature has fallen when worldly status and bodily pleasure become people's highest goals!

Disappointment and trouble inevitably accompany such pursuits.

The person best placed to enjoy even this present life is the one who most carefully obeys God's commands.

Yet amid these human practices, we should recognize God's wise and merciful providence, carrying forward purposes both hidden and holy.

A change in social position never excuses us from our duties to our parents or to people who have fulfilled a parent's role in our lives.

Mordecai discovers a conspiracy (verses 21–23)

Good citizens must not conceal a plot they know about against the ruler or the public peace.

Mordecai received no immediate reward for exposing the conspiracy.

But a written record preserved his service.

Similarly, people who serve Christ may not receive their reward until the resurrection of the righteous.

Yet God keeps an account of every act of faithful work and loving service.

He does not unjustly forget any of it.

Those who serve God should faithfully discharge every trust and remain watchful for the interests of those who employ them.

Even if they appear to be overlooked now, their service will be remembered later.

Nothing we do is forgotten. Even hidden thoughts are recorded in enduring books (Revelation 20:12).

We see to what absurd practices those came, who were destitute of Divine revelation, and what need there was of the gospel of Christ, to purify men from the lusts of the flesh, and to bring them back to the original institution of marriage. Esther was preferred as queen. Those who suggest that Esther committed sin to come at this dignity, do not consider the custom of those times and countries. Every one that the king took was married to him, and was his wife, though of a lower rank. But how low is human nature sunk, when such as these are the leading pursuits and highest worldly happiness of men! Disappointment and vexation must follow; and he most wisely consults his enjoyment, even in this present life, who most exactly obeys the precepts of the Divine law. But let us turn to consider the wise and merciful providence of God, carrying on his deep but holy designs in the midst of all this. And let no change in our condition be a pretext for forgetting our duties to parents, or the friends who have stood in their place.
[Esth.2.21-Esth.2.23]

Good subjects must not conceal any bad design they know of against the prince, or the public peace. Mordecai was not rewarded at the time, but a remembrance was written. Thus, with respect to those who serve Christ, though their recompence is not till the resurrection of the just, yet an account is kept of their work of faith and labour of love, which God is not unrighteous to forget. The servant of God must be faithful to every trust, and watchful for those who employ him. If he appear to be neglected now, he will be remembered hereafter. None of our actions can be forgotten; even our most secret thoughts are written in lasting registers, [Rev.20.12] Re 20:12.

Haman seeks to destroy the Jews (verses 1–6)

Mordecai refused to show Haman the reverence demanded of him.

The Jewish faith forbade giving any human being honors that resembled idolatrous worship, especially a wicked person like Haman.

Human beings naturally tend toward idolatry: self is our favorite idol, and we enjoy being treated as though everything belonged to us.

Faith does not abolish good manners. On the contrary, it teaches us to give appropriate honor to those who deserve it.

Yet someone belonging to Zion must regard a wicked person like Haman as contemptible, not only inwardly but in judgment and conduct (Psalm 15:4).

True believers cannot obey decrees or follow fashions that violate God's commands.

They must obey God rather than human beings, leaving the consequences in his hands.

Haman became furious.

His plot reflected the spirit of the murderer from the beginning, whose hatred toward Christ and the church rules those who follow him.

Haman obtains a decree (verses 7–15)

Anyone who knows the human heart and human history should understand how a ruler could agree to a proposal so cruel and contrary to his own interests.

We should be thankful for mild and just government.

Haman tried to discover, through his superstition, an auspicious day for the massacre he intended.

God's wisdom used that folly to accomplish his own purposes.

The lot Haman cast delayed the date of the planned killing and thereby helped bring about his defeat.

The episode displays God's particular Providence in human affairs and his care for the church.

Haman feared that the king might be troubled by what he had approved, so he encouraged him to continue drinking.

People often try to drown their convictions and harden their own hearts and others' hearts through intoxication.

Everything seemed to be moving toward Haman's goal.

Yet God can allow sinners to progress far in their plans before his unseen, almighty power turns them back.

Even the strongest attack against Jehovah is vain.

If Haman had destroyed the Jewish people, how could God's promises and prophecies about the world's Redeemer have been fulfilled?

God's everlasting covenant would have had to fail first.
classic_reading:

Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
Haman seeks to destroy the Jews. | (1-6) |
He obtains a decree against the Jews. | (7-15) |
Verses 1-6
Mordecai refused to reverence Haman. The religion of a Jew forbade him to give honours to any mortal man which savoured of idolatry, especially to so wicked a man as Haman. By nature all are idolaters; self is our favourite idol, we are pleased to be treated as if every thing were at our disposal. Though religion by no means destroys good manners, but teaches us to render honour to whom honour is due, yet by a citizen of Zion, not only in his heart, but in his eyes, such a vile person as Haman was, is contemned, [Ps.15.4] Psa 15:4. The true believer cannot obey edicts, or conform to fashions, which break the law of God. He must obey God rather than man, and leave the consequences to him. Haman was full of wrath. His device was inspired by that wicked spirit, who has been a murderer from the beginning; whose enmity to Christ and his church, governs all his children.
[Esth.3.7-Esth.3.15]
Verses 7-15
Without some acquaintance with the human heart, and the history of mankind, we should not think that any prince could consent to a dreadful proposal, so hurtful to himself. Let us be thankful for mild and just government. Haman inquires, according to his own superstitions, how to find a lucky day for the designed massacre! God's wisdom serves its own purposes by men's folly. Haman has appealed to the lot, and the lot, by delaying the execution, gives judgment against him. The event explains the doctrine of a particular providence over all the affairs of men, and the care of God over his church. Haman was afraid lest the king's conscience should smite him for what he had done; to prevent which, he kept him drinking. This cursed method many often take to drown convictions, and to harden their own hearts, and the hearts of others, in sin. All appeared in a favourable train to accomplish the project. But though sinners are permitted to proceed to the point they aim at, an unseen but almighty Power turns them back. How vain and contemptible are the strongest assaults against Jehovah! Had Haman obtained his wish, and the Jewish nation perished, what must have become of all the promises? How could the prophecies concerning the great Redeemer of the world have been fulfilled? Thus the everlasting covenant itself must have failed, before this diabolical project could take place.

The Jews grieve over the decree (verses 1–4)

Mordecai openly acknowledged his connection with the Jewish people.

Trouble affecting God's church should weigh more heavily upon us than private misfortune.

It is especially painful to know that our own conduct has contributed to other people's suffering.

God will preserve those whose sensitive consciences expose them to danger.

Esther decides to intercede (verses 5–17)

We naturally shrink from tasks that may cost us dearly or endanger us.

But when Christ's cause and people need our service, we must take up our cross and follow him.

Christians should be corrected when they seek personal comfort or safety at the expense of the public good.

The Persian law against approaching the king uninvited was explicit and widely known.

It is not like that at the court of the King of kings.

We may always come boldly to the throne of grace, expecting God's peaceful answer to faithful prayer.

Through Jesus' blood, we are welcome even into the holiest place.

God's Providence had arranged for the king's affection toward Esther to cool by this time, according to Henry's interpretation.

This made her faith and courage face a greater test and the king's eventual kindness more remarkable.

Haman, Henry supposes, had probably also tried to turn the king against her.

Mordecai believed that the Jewish people's cause would succeed one way or another.

Esther could therefore undertake her duty with confidence.

This was the language of strong faith, trusting God's promise even when hope seemed impossible.

Someone who tries to preserve life through sinful methods instead of trusting God while doing duty will lose it by sin.

Esther's royal position had been prepared through Providence for precisely such service.

Gratitude obliged her to act for God and his people.

Otherwise, she would fail to fulfill the purpose of her promotion.

God's wise counsel is at work in every event, directing it toward the church's ultimate good.

Each of us should consider why God has placed us where we are and seek to fulfill our calling before the opportunity passes.

Once we have committed ourselves and our cause to God, we may courageously undertake his service.

Every earthly danger is small compared with the danger of losing our souls.

Sinners who tremble before God can resemble Esther before the king: they fear entrusting themselves entirely to his mercy.

Let such a person approach with earnest prayer.

God will receive them even more graciously than Ahasuerus received Esther.

God's cause will prevail, and those united to it are safe.

Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The Jews lament their danger. | (1-4) |
Esther undertakes to plead for the Jews. | (5-17) |
Verses 1-4
Mordecai avowed his relation to the Jews. Public calamities, that oppress the church of God, should affect our hearts more than any private affliction, and it is peculiarly distressing to occasion sufferings to others. God will keep those that are exposed to evil by the tenderness of their consciences.
[Esth.4.5-Esth.4.17]
Verses 5-17
We are prone to shrink from services that are attended with peril or loss. But when the cause of Christ and his people demand it, we must take up our cross, and follow him. When Christians are disposed to consult their own ease or safety, rather than the public good, they should be blamed. The law was express, all knew it. It is not thus in the court of the King of kings: to the footstool of his throne of grace we may always come boldly, and may be sure of an answer of peace to the prayer of faith. We are welcome, even into the holiest, through the blood of Jesus. Providence so ordered it, that, just then, the king's affections had cooled toward Esther; her faith and courage thereby were the more tried; and God's goodness in the favour she now found with the king, thereby shone the brighter. Haman no doubt did what he could to set the king against her. Mordecai suggests, that it was a cause which, one way or other, would certainly be carried, and which therefore she might safely venture in. This was the language of strong faith, which staggered not at the promise when the danger was most threatening, but against hope believed in hope. He that by sinful devices will save his life, and will not trust God with it in the way of duty, shall lose it in the way of sin. Divine Providence had regard to this matter, in bringing Esther to be queen. Therefore thou art bound in gratitude to do this service for God and his church, else thou dost not answer the end of thy being raised up. There is wise counsel and design in all the providences of God, which will prove that they are all intended for the good of the church. We should, every one, consider for what end God has put us in the place where we are, and study to answer that end: and take care that we do not let it slip. Having solemnly commended our souls and our cause to God, we may venture upon his service. All dangers are trifling compared with the danger of losing our souls. But the trembling sinner is often as much afraid of casting himself, without reserve, upon the Lord's free mercy, as Esther was of coming before the king. Let him venture, as she did, with earnest prayer and supplication, and he shall fare as well and better than she did. The cause of God must prevail: we are safe in being united to it.

The king receives Esther (verses 1–8)

Esther had prevailed with God, as Jacob did, and therefore found favor with a human ruler too.

Whoever is willing to lose life for God will save it, or receive a better life.

The king encouraged her.

Let that encourage us to pray continually and not give up.

Esther approached a proud, imperious man.

We approach the God of love and grace.

Esther was not invited, but we are invited: the Spirit and the bride say, “Come.”

She faced a law against her.

We have many promises in our favor: Ask, and it will be given.

She had no friend to accompany her or plead for her.

Indeed, the king's current favorite was her enemy.

But we have an Advocate before the Father, one in whom the Father delights.

Therefore, approach the throne of grace boldly.

God moved Esther to postpone her request for one more day.

She did not know what would happen that very night, but God did.

Haman plans Mordecai's execution (verses 9–14)

Haman's behavior illustrates Proverbs 21:24.

People who admire and flatter themselves are actually deceiving themselves.

The higher Haman rose, the less patiently he endured even a small sign of disrespect.

Mordecai's conduct ruined his pleasure in everything else.

A slight insult that a humble person might scarcely notice can torment a proud person almost to madness.

Those determined to be unhappy will always find something to make them unhappy.

Proud people can possess nearly everything they desire, yet if they lack one thing, all the rest becomes worthless in their eyes.

Many admire the wealthy and powerful who surround themselves with splendor.

But this is a mistaken view of happiness.

Many poor families in small cottages have far less anxiety than wealthy people living amid supposed advantages.

Whoever does not know Christ is poor, however much wealth that person possesses, because the only true riches are missing.

Verses 1-8
Esther having had power with God, and prevailing, like Jacob, had power with men too. He that will lose his life for God, shall save it, or find it in a better life. The king encouraged her. Let us from this be encouraged to pray always to our God, and not to faint. Esther came to a proud, imperious man; but we come to the God of love and grace. She was not called, but we are; the Spirit says, Come, and the Bride says, Come. She had a law against her, we have a promise, many a promise, in favour of us; Ask, and it shall be given you. She had no friend to go with her, or to plead for her; on the contrary, he that was then the king's favourite, was her enemy; but we have an Advocate with the Father, in whom he is well pleased. Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace. God put it into Esther's heart to delay her petition a day longer; she knew not, but God did, what was to happen in that very night.
[Esth.5.9-Esth.5.14]

This account of Haman is a comment upon [Prov.21.24] Pr 21:24. Self-admirers and self-flatterers are really self-deceivers. Haman, the higher he is lifted up, the more impatient he is of contempt, and the more enraged at it. The affront from Mordecai spoiled all. A slight affront, which a humble man would scarcely notice, will torment a proud man, even to madness, and will mar all his comforts. Those disposed to be uneasy, will never want something to be uneasy at. Such are proud men; though they have much to their mind, if they have not all to their mind, it is as nothing to them. Many call the proud happy, who display pomp and make a show; but this is a mistaken thought. Many poor cottagers feel far less uneasiness than the rich, with all their fancied advantages around them. The man who knows not Christ, is poor though he be rich, because he is utterly destitute of that which alone is true riches.

Providence brings Mordecai to the king's attention (verses 1–3)

God's Providence governs even the smallest human concerns.

Not even a sparrow falls to the ground without him.

Consider the steps through which Providence brought Mordecai into a place of honor.

The king could not sleep because God had a purpose to accomplish through his wakefulness.

Nothing suggests an illness interrupted his sleep.

God simply withheld it, though sleep itself is a gift from him.

A man who could command 127 provinces could not command one hour of sleep.

Haman advises the king to honor Mordecai (verses 4–11)

See how pride deceives people.

Nothing reveals the deceitfulness of our hearts more clearly than our exaggerated opinion of ourselves and our achievements.

We must continually watch and pray against this tendency.

Haman assumed the king could not possibly honor anyone but him.

He was mistaken.

We should be cautious about assuming the admiration other people express is as great as it appears.

That caution protects us against self-importance and excessive dependence upon people's favor.

What a shock Haman received when the king ordered him to honor Mordecai the Jew, the very person Haman hated most and was planning to kill!

Haman returns humiliated (verses 12–14)

Mordecai did not become proud because of his new honor.

He returned to his place and his duty.

Honor is well given to those who do not believe themselves above ordinary work.

Haman, however, could not bear the humiliation.

What real harm had Mordecai's honor done him?

Yet something that scarcely interrupts a humble person's sleep can break a proud person's heart.

Haman's wife and friends now foretold his downfall.

They recognized plainly that the scattered Jewish people enjoyed God's special protection.

But they were miserable comforters.

They did not tell Haman to repent, only that destruction was unavoidable.

God's wisdom appears in the timing of his church's deliverance, which brings glory to his own name.

Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
Providence recommends Mordecai to the king's favour. | (1-3) |
Haman's counsel honours Mordecai. | (4-11) |

Verses 1-3
The providence of God rules over the smallest concerns of men. Not a sparrow falls to the ground without him. Trace the steps which Providence took towards the advancement of Mordecai. The king could not sleep when Providence had a design to serve, in keeping him awake. We read of no illness that broke his sleep, but God, whose gift sleep is, withheld it from him. He who commanded a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, could not command one hour's sleep.
[Esth.6.4-Esth.6.11]
Verses 4-11
See how men's pride deceives them. The deceitfulness of our own hearts appears in nothing more than in the conceit we have of ourselves and our own performances: against which we should constantly watch and pray. Haman thought the king loved and valued no one but himself, but he was deceived. We should suspect that the esteem which others profess for us, is not so great as it seems to be, that we may not think too well of ourselves, nor trust too much in others. How Haman is struck, when the king bids him do honour to Mordecai the Jew, the very man whom he hated above all men, whose ruin he was now designing!
[Esth.6.12-Esth.6.14]
Verses 12-14
Mordecai was not puffed up with his honours, he returned to his place and the duty of it. Honour is well bestowed on those that do not think themselves above their business. But Haman could not bear it. What harm had it done him? But that will break a proud man's heart, which will not break a humble man's sleep. His doom was, out of this event, read to him by his wife and his friends. They plainly confessed that the Jews, though scattered through the nations, were special objects of Divine care. Miserable comforters are they all; they did not advise Haman to repent, but foretold his fate as unavoidable. The wisdom of God is seen, in timing the means of his church's deliverance, so as to manifest his own glory.

Esther accuses Haman (verses 1–6)

If our love of life causes us to plead earnestly before people who can only kill the body, how much more fervently should we pray to God, who can judge both body and soul!

How earnestly should we pray for the salvation of family, friends and everyone around us!

When petitioning powerful people, we must sometimes hold back even just complaints for fear of offending them.

But when we approach the King of kings with reverence, we cannot ask or expect too much.

Although we deserve only God's judgment, he is both willing and able to do far more than we can ask or imagine.

Haman dies on the gallows he built (verses 7–10)

The king became angry.

People who act according to their own will sometimes later condemn themselves for their actions.

When anger rises, we should delay making decisions and thus show control over ourselves and obedience to sound reason.

People who are proudest and most overbearing when powerful often become the most servile and timid when their position collapses.

The day will come when those who hate and persecute God's chosen people will gladly seek help from them.

The king returned even angrier with Haman.

His attendants were ready to carry out his judgment.

How little confidence proud people can have in the influence they imagine they possess!

The enemies of God's church have often been trapped by their own schemes.

Such judgments display the Lord's righteousness.

The king's anger was finally satisfied.

Few would pity Haman for dying on the gallows he had constructed for another; Henry calls readers to recognize God's justice in the outcome.

Let those who commit evil tremble, turn to the Lord and seek forgiveness through Jesus' blood.

Esther accuses Haman. | (1-6) |
Haman hanged on his own gallows. | (7-10) |

If the love of life causes earnest pleadings with those that can only kill the body, how fervent should our prayers be to Him, who is able to destroy both body and soul in hell! How should we pray for the salvation of our relatives, friends, and all around us! When we petition great men, we must be cautious not to give them offence; even just complaints must often be kept back. But when we approach the King of kings with reverence, we cannot ask or expect too much. Though nothing but wrath be our due, God is able and willing to do exceeding abundantly, even beyond all we can ask or think.
[Esth.7.7-Esth.7.10]
Verses 7-10
The king was angry: those that do things with self-will, reflect upon them afterward with self-reproach. When angry, we should pause before we come to any resolution, and thus rule our own spirits, and show that we are governed by reason. Those that are most haughty and insolent when in power and prosperity, commonly, like Haman, are the most abject and poor-spirited when brought down. The day is coming when those that hate and persecute God's chosen ones, would gladly be beholden to them. The king returns yet more angry against Haman. Those about him were ready to put his wrath into execution. How little can proud men be sure of the interest they think they have! The enemies of God's church have often been thus taken in their own craftiness. The Lord is known by such judgments. Then was the king's wrath pacified, and not till then. And who pities Haman hanged on his own gallows? who does not rather rejoice in the Divine righteousness displayed in the destruction his own art brought upon him? Let the workers of iniquity tremble, turn to the Lord, and seek pardon through the blood of Jesus.

Mordecai receives Haman's former position (verses 1 and 2)

Esther intended to use for good what Haman had meant to use for evil.

The responsibility and trust the king had given Haman now passed to Mordecai—a welcome change.

See the emptiness of accumulating treasure on earth.

The person who stores up wealth cannot know who will eventually enjoy it.

Had Haman known that his most hated enemy would take control of everything he worked to acquire, even looking at his possessions would have brought distress instead of pleasure.

We should therefore seek riches that cannot be left behind, but will accompany us into eternity.

Esther pleads for her people (verses 3–14)

With the church of God in danger, earnest action was necessary.

Though Esther herself was safe, she fell before the king and begged him to rescue her people.

No tears are recorded when she sought protection for her own life.

But when her people's safety was at stake, she wept.

Such compassion and tender concern most closely resemble Christ.

Persian government treated royal decrees as unchangeable and impossible to recall.

Far from proving the wisdom of its rulers, this displayed their pride and folly.

It resembled the arrogant desire to be like gods.

Only God has the right to declare what cannot be changed or withdrawn.

Nevertheless, a solution was found: a second decree permitted the Jews to defend themselves.

The decree was published in the languages of all the provinces.

If earthly rulers make their laws available in languages their subjects understand, how could Christians justify keeping God's words and commands in a language his servants cannot understand?

Mordecai is honored and the Jews rejoice (verses 15–17)

Mordecai now wore splendid royal clothing.

This mattered not for its own sake but as evidence of the king's approval and of God's favor toward the church.

A country is fortunate when positions of honor are filled by people of genuine devotion.

When God's church prospers, many will join it who would avoid identifying with it during persecution.

When believers experience peace and walk in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, they grow in number.

Satan's attempts to destroy the church ultimately help bring more people into genuine Christian faith.

Verses 1-2
What Haman would have done mischief with, Esther will do good with. All the trust the king had reposed in Haman, he now placed in Mordecai: a happy change. See the vanity of laying up treasure upon earth; he that heapeth up riches, knoweth not who shall gather them. With what little pleasure, nay, with what constant vexation, would Haman have looked upon his estate, if he could have foreseen that Mordecai, the man he hated above all men in the world, should have rule over all that wherein he had laboured! It is our interest to make sure of those riches which will not be left behind, but which will go with us to another world.
[Esth.8.3-Esth.8.14]
Verses 3-14
It was time to be earnest, when the church of God was at stake. Esther, though safe herself, fell down and begged for the deliverance of her people. We read of no tears when she begged for her own life, but although she was sure of that, she wept for her people. Tears of pity and tenderness are the most Christ-like. According to the constitution of the Persian government, no law or decree could be repealed or recalled. This is so far from speaking to the wisdom and honour of the Medes and Persians, that it clearly shows their pride and folly. This savours of that old presumption which ruined all, We will be as gods! It is God's prerogative not to repent, or to say what can never be altered or unsaid. Yet a way was found, by another decree, to authorize the Jews to stand upon their defence. The decree was published in the languages of all the provinces. Shall all the subjects of an earthly prince have his decrees in languages they understand, and shall God's oracles and laws be locked up from any of his servants in an unknown tongue?
[Esth.8.15-Esth.8.17]
Verses 15-17
Mordecai's robes now were rich. These things are not worth notice, but as marks of the king's favour, and the fruit of God's favour to his church. It is well with a land, when ensigns of dignity are made the ornaments of serious piety. When the church prospers, many will join it, who will be shy of it when in trouble. When believers have rest, and walk in the fear of the Lord, and the comfort of the Holy Ghost, they will be multiplied. And the attempts of Satan to destroy the church, always tend to increase the number of true Christians.

The Jews are delivered (verses 1–19)

The enemies of the Jews expected to defeat them under the earlier royal decree.

Had those enemies not tried to harm God's people, they would not themselves have suffered.

The Jews acted together and strengthened one another.

We should likewise remain firm in one spirit and with one mind, standing together against the spiritual enemies who seek to rob us of faith, a possession worth more than life.

The Jews refused to enrich themselves through plunder.

This honored their faith by showing that they sought only their own preservation.

In every circumstance God's people should be compassionate and free from selfish motives.

They may wisely decline advantages they could lawfully claim.

The Jews celebrated the day after their work ended.

Whenever God grants a great mercy, we should respond promptly with thanksgiving.

The Feast of Purim is established (verses 20–32)

The continued observance of Jewish festivals publicly testifies to the truth of the Old Testament Scriptures.

Henry argues from that truth that the promised Messiah has already come and that Jesus of Nazareth alone fulfills the promise.

Purim was established through public authority, yet under God's guidance by the Holy Spirit.

The name Purim comes from a Persian word meaning “lot.”

That name reminded the Jews how the Almighty used even pagan superstition to carry out his purposes.

When we remember God's mercies, we should also remember the fears and distress from which he delivered us.

We must not forget personal mercies and thereby lose their comfort or withhold the glory owed to God.

May he teach us to rejoice with a holy joy that anticipates and prepares us for heaven's happiness.

Every act of divine goodness toward us creates a fresh obligation to do good to others, especially to those in greatest need.

Above all, our redemption through Christ calls us to mercy and generosity (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Verses 1-19
The enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them by the former edict. If they had attempted nothing against the people of God, they would not themselves have suffered. The Jews, acting together, strengthened one another. Let us learn to stand fast in one spirit, and with one mind, striving together against the enemies of our souls, who endeavour to rob us of our faith, which is more precious than our lives. The Jews, to the honour of their religion, showed contempt of wordly wealth, that they might make it appear they desired nothing except their own preservation. In every case the people of God should manifest humanity and disinterestedness, frequently refusing advantages which might lawfully be obtained. The Jews celebrated their festival the day after they had finished their work. When we have received great mercies from God, we ought to be speedy in making thankful returns to him.
[Esth.9.20-Esth.9.32]
Verses 20-32
The observance of the Jewish feasts, is a public declaration of the truth of the Old Testament Scriptures. And as the Old Testament Scriptures are true, the Messiah expected by the Jews is come long ago; and none but Jesus of Nazareth can be that Messiah. The festival was appointed by authority, yet under the direction of the Spirit of God. It was called the feast of Purim, from a Persian word, which signifies a lot. The name of this festival would remind them of the almighty power of the God of Israel, who served his own purposes by the superstitions of the heathen. In reviewing our mercies, we should advert to former fears and distresses. When our mercies are personal, we should not by forgetfulness lose the comfort of them, or withhold from the Lord the glory due to his name. May the Lord teach us to rejoice, with that holy joy which anticipates and prepares for the blessedness of heaven. Every instance of Divine goodness to ourselves, is a new obligation laid on us to do good, to those especially who most need our bounty. Above all, redemption by Christ binds us to be merciful, [2Cor.8.9] 2Co 8:9.

Greatness of Ahasuerus—Mordecai's advancement.

Mordecai's greatness and service

Many more stories of Ahasuerus's greatness could have been told.

They were recorded in Persian chronicles that have long since disappeared.

But Scripture will remain as long as time endures.

The Holy Spirit considers the concerns of the Lord's despised worshipers more important than the exploits of even the most impressive earthly ruler.

Mordecai was truly great, and his higher position gave him greater opportunities to do good.

He did not deny his people, the Jews, and undoubtedly continued in the true faith.

He sought not his own wealth but his people's welfare.

Few have the opportunity to do as much good as Mordecai.

Yet all have the ability to do harm, and everyone has some ability to do good.

We are not required to do what lies beyond our abilities or outside the responsibilities of our position.

But we are all called to live according to the spirit displayed by the faithful people whose examples Scripture records.

If we live by faith in Christ, we will actively use whatever opportunities and abilities he gives us to promote his glory and other people's highest good.

Genuine faith works through love.

Wait upon God in faith and prayer.

The final outcome will be secure and glorious, because our salvation is certain through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Chapter 10
Greatness of Ahasuerus--Mordecai's advancement.
--Many instances of the grandeur of Ahasuerus might have been given: these were written in the Persian chronicles, which are long since lost, while the sacred writings will live till time shall be no more. The concerns of the despised worshippers of the Lord are deemed more important by the Holy Spirit, than the exploits of the most illustrious monarch on earth. Mordecai was truly great, and his greatness gave him opportunities of doing the more good. He did not disown his people the Jews, and no doubt kept to the true religion. He did not seek his own wealth, but the welfare of his people. Few have it in their power to do so much good as Mordecai; but all have it in their power to do hurt, and who has it not in his power to do some good? We are not required to do what is not in our power, or is unsuited to our station; but all are bound to live under the influence of the tempers displayed in the saints, whose examples are recorded in the Bible. If we live by the faith of Christ, we shall be active according to the ability and opportunities he gives us, in promoting his glory and the best interests of men. If our faith be genuine, it will work by love. Wait in faith and prayer, and the event will be safe and glorious; our salvation is sure, through our Lord Jesus Christ.
